Acts 1: Forty days after the resurrection, Jesus is taken up from the mount of Olives (Acts 1:3, 12), about AD 30 or 33. Acts is the second volume to Theophilus, after Luke (Acts 1:1); it ends with Paul in Rome about AD 62.
Acts 2: On the day of Pentecost, fifty days after Passover, Jews from across the Roman and Parthian world are in Jerusalem (Acts 2:9–11).
Acts 3: Peter and John go to the temple "at the hour of prayer, being the ninth hour" (Acts 3:1), about 3 p.m.
Acts 4: Annas, Caiaphas, and the high priest's family question Peter and John (Acts 4:6).
Acts 5: The council arrests the apostles. Gamaliel, a leading Pharisee, recalls the revolts of Theudas and Judas of Galilee (Acts 5:36–37).
Acts 6: Greek-speaking Jewish believers in Jerusalem complain about their widows, and seven men are chosen.
Acts 7: Stephen speaks before the council and is stoned outside the city; Saul looks on (Acts 7:58), in the mid-30s AD.
Acts 8: Persecution scatters the church through Judea and Samaria. Philip meets an official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, on the road to Gaza.
Acts 9: Saul travels to Damascus, about 135 miles north of Jerusalem, and is converted. Peter heals at Lydda and Joppa.
Acts 10: Cornelius, a centurion, lives at Caesarea, the Roman capital of Judea on the coast. Peter is staying at Joppa.
Acts 11: Believers are first called Christians at Antioch in Syria (Acts 11:26). A famine is foretold that "came to pass in the days of Claudius Caesar" (Acts 11:28), emperor AD 41–54.
Acts 12: Herod Agrippa I kills James and imprisons Peter, then dies at Caesarea (Acts 12:23) in AD 44.
Acts 13: Barnabas and Saul sail from Antioch to Cyprus, then go to Perga and Antioch in Pisidia, on the first journey, about AD 46–48.
Acts 14: Paul and Barnabas preach in Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe in the region of Lycaonia, then return to Antioch.
Acts 15: The apostles and elders meet in Jerusalem, about AD 49, to decide whether Gentile believers must be circumcised.
Acts 16: On the second journey, Paul crosses from Troas to Macedonia and founds the church at Philippi, a Roman colony, about AD 50.
Acts 17: Paul preaches in Thessalonica, Berea, and Athens, where he speaks at the Areopagus.
Acts 18: Paul stays eighteen months in Corinth (Acts 18:11). Gallio is proconsul of Achaia, which an inscription at Delphi dates to about AD 51–52.
Acts 19: On the third journey, Paul spends over two years in Ephesus (Acts 19:10), about AD 52–55, home of the great temple of Diana.
Acts 20: Paul travels through Macedonia and Greece, stays at Troas, and meets the Ephesian elders at Miletus, hurrying to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost (Acts 20:16).
Acts 21: Paul arrives in Jerusalem about AD 57 and is seized in the temple. Roman soldiers from the castle (the Antonia fortress) rescue him.
Acts 22: Paul speaks to the crowd in Hebrew from the castle stairs and claims his Roman citizenship.
Acts 23: Paul is brought before the council, then sent by night to Felix, the governor, at Caesarea.
Acts 24: Paul is tried before Felix, governor of Judea about AD 52–59, and held two years (Acts 24:27).
Acts 25: Porcius Festus succeeds Felix, about AD 59. Paul appeals to Caesar, then Nero.
Acts 26: Paul speaks before Herod Agrippa II and his sister Bernice at Caesarea.
Acts 27: Paul sails for Italy after "the fast" (Acts 27:9), the Day of Atonement in autumn, and is shipwrecked on Malta, about AD 59–60.
Acts 28: After three months on Malta, Paul reaches Rome by the Appian Way and lives two years under guard in his own rented house (Acts 28:11, 30), about AD 60–62.
